title: Statutory Compliance for Small Stock Slaughter

lessons.title: The laws that govern slaughter
lessons.html:
Why there are laws

Laws protect the people who eat meat, the animals, the workers and the environment. An abattoir that breaks the law can be fined or closed. Workers who break the rules can be disciplined. You do not need to know every word of these laws, but you must know what they mean for your work.

The main laws for a small stock slaughterer

LawWhat it means for you
Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000Slaughter at registered abattoirs; hygienic work; meat inspection before and after slaughter; humane slaughter
Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962No cruelty to animals; handle sheep and goats humanely
Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984Controlled diseases must be reported; movement controls must be followed
Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993A safe workplace; workers must follow safety rules and report hazards
National Water Act 36 of 1998Dirty water from the abattoir must not pollute rivers and groundwater

There are also regulations under the Meat Safety Act that give detailed rules for abattoir hygiene and slaughter. Your abattoir's procedures are written to follow them.

Who checks

  • Meat inspectors and veterinarians check animals and meat every day.
  • The provincial veterinary services audit and register abattoirs.
  • Inspectors from the Department of Employment and Labour may check health and safety.

lessons.title: What compliance looks like on the slaughter floor
lessons.html:
Compliance every day

Compliance means following the law and the rules. On the slaughter floor it means doing small things right every time.

Meat safety rules

  • Every sheep and goat is inspected before slaughter. Animals set aside by the meat inspector are not slaughtered with the others.
  • Every carcass, head and its organs are presented for inspection together and kept matched.
  • You never remove, cut out or hide a sign of disease before the inspector has seen it.
  • Condemned meat is put into marked bins and locked away until it is destroyed. It must never be taken home or sold.
  • Only passed carcasses get the inspection stamp.

Animal welfare rules

  • Sheep and goats are handled calmly. Never lift sheep by the wool or goats by the horns.
  • Every animal is properly stunned before bleeding, unless the abattoir is approved for religious slaughter and follows the approved procedure.
  • Animals in the lairage get water.

Safety rules

  • Wear your protective equipment.
  • Use only equipment you are trained for.
  • Report injuries, near-misses and unsafe conditions.

Hygiene rules

  • Clean protective clothing, hand washing, no jewellery.
  • Sterilise knives.
  • Keep dirty and clean areas separate.

lessons.title: Records, documents and your responsibility
lessons.html:
Records the law needs

Abattoirs must be able to show what they did. Records prove compliance. Common records in a small stock abattoir:

  • Receiving records: owner, number of animals, where they came from.
  • Proof of ownership: livestock must arrive with documents showing who owns them. This helps to stop stock theft.
  • Kill sheets: how many animals were slaughtered, carcass numbers and masses.
  • Inspection records: kept by the meat inspector.
  • Condemnation records: what was condemned and why.
  • Temperature logs: chiller temperatures.
  • Cleaning records: what was cleaned, when, and by whom.

Stock theft

Stock theft is a big problem for South African sheep and goat farmers. If animals arrive without proper ownership documents, or the documents do not match the animals' marks or numbers, report it to your supervisor. Do not slaughter them until the supervisor says so.

Your responsibility

  1. Know the rules for your station.
  2. Follow them every time.
  3. Fill in records honestly.
  4. Report anything that is not right.
  5. Follow every instruction from the meat inspector.

If you break the rules, for example by taking condemned meat or hiding a dirty carcass, you can lose your job, and the abattoir can lose its registration. Worse, people can get sick.

Key points

  • The Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 is the main law for abattoir slaughter and inspection.
  • The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 forbids cruelty to animals.
  • Present every carcass and its organs to the meat inspector and never hide disease.
  • Condemned meat must never be taken or sold.
  • Report animals that arrive without proper ownership documents.
  • Keep records honest and complete.
